glossary.definition: The ninth month of the Islamic lunar calendar, during which Muslims observe fasting from dawn to sunset as one of the Five Pillars of Islam.
The pre-dawn meal eaten before beginning the daily fast. It's recommended to eat suhoor as close to dawn as possible for maximum energy during fasting hours.
The evening meal that breaks the daily fast at sunset. Traditionally begins with dates and water, following the Prophet's practice.
The dawn prayer and also the time when fasting begins each day. The call to Fajr prayer signals the start of the fasting period.
The sunset prayer and the time when fasting ends each day. The call to Maghrib prayer signals it's time for iftar.
Special evening prayers performed during Ramadan after the Isha (night) prayer. These prayers involve recitation of the Quran.
Obligatory charitable giving, one of the Five Pillars of Islam. During Ramadan, many Muslims calculate and pay their annual zakat.
Voluntary charitable giving beyond zakat. The rewards for sadaqah are believed to be multiplied during Ramadan.
The Arabic word for fasting. Sawm is one of the Five Pillars of Islam and involves abstaining from food, drink, and other physical needs from dawn to sunset.
The Night of Power or Decree, believed to fall within the last ten nights of Ramadan. It commemorates the night the Quran was first revealed.
The Festival of Breaking Fast, a three-day celebration marking the end of Ramadan. It begins with a special prayer and involves family gatherings, gift-giving, and festive meals.
The holy book of Islam, believed to be the word of God revealed to Prophet Muhammad. Ramadan is the month when its revelation began.
Personal supplication or prayer to God. The moment just before breaking fast is considered an especially blessed time for dua.
Intention. Making the intention to fast is an essential part of the fasting practice, typically made before Fajr.
A charitable donation given before Eid prayer, typically the value of one meal per family member, to ensure everyone can celebrate Eid.

fastingRules.title: What Does NOT Invalidate the Fast
rules: Eating or drinking by accident (forgetting you're fasting)
Brushing teeth (being careful not to swallow)
Receiving injections or blood tests (for medical purposes)

fastingRules.title: Who is Exempt from Fasting
rules: Those who are ill or have medical conditions
fastingRules.note: Those who are temporarily exempt should make up missed fasts later. Those permanently exempt may pay fidya (feeding a poor person for each day missed).

healthBenefits.title: Metabolic Health
healthBenefits.description: Intermittent fasting can improve insulin sensitivity, blood pressure, and reduce oxidative stress markers.

healthBenefits.title: Weight Management
healthBenefits.description: Studies show intermittent fasting can lead to 3-8% body weight reduction over 3-24 weeks.

healthBenefits.title: Cardiovascular Benefits
healthBenefits.description: Research shows fasting can improve cardiovascular risk factors including blood pressure and cholesterol levels.

healthBenefits.title: Cellular Health
healthBenefits.description: Fasting triggers autophagy (cellular cleaning processes) which may have anti-aging effects.

healthBenefits.title: Brain Health
healthBenefits.description: Intermittent fasting may support cognitive function and potentially reduce risk of neurodegenerative diseases.
